big_idea: Organizations should deliberately design their team structures -- not just their processes -- around fast flow of value, because the shape of your teams will eventually determine the shape of your software whether you plan it or not.

tool.label: The Four Fundamental Team Topologies
tool.text: Skelton and Pais argue nearly every team should map to one of four types. Stream-aligned teams own a slice of business value end-to-end with no handoffs. Platform teams build internal, self-service capabilities that let stream-aligned teams move faster. Enabling teams are temporary specialists who help other teams close a capability gap and then move on. Complicated-subsystem teams handle a component that genuinely requires deep specialist knowledge. Teams interact only through three modes -- collaboration, X-as-a-service, and facilitation -- chosen deliberately and revisited over time.
tool.note: Reviewers, including engineer Jacob Kaplan-Moss, have pushed back on the claim that these are the only four team types an organization ever needs, calling some edge cases a stretch to categorize; the framework is easiest to apply in mid-size-to-large software organizations.

ideas.title: Conway's Law as a design input, not just an observation
ideas.text: The book treats Conway's original observation as something leaders should actively exploit, deliberately shaping teams to produce the software architecture they want.

ideas.title: Cognitive load as a team-sizing constraint
ideas.text: A team's scope should be bounded by what its members can hold in their heads at once; overloading a team with too many unrelated systems is a primary cause of slow delivery.

ideas.title: Team API
ideas.text: Each team is framed as exposing a team API -- the interfaces, documentation, and practices other teams use to interact with it.

ideas.title: Thinnest viable platform
ideas.text: Platform teams are advised to build the smallest platform that removes friction for stream-aligned teams, avoiding an over-engineered internal platform that becomes its own bottleneck.

ideas.title: Interaction modes have a lifecycle
ideas.text: Collaboration mode is meant to be temporary and high-bandwidth, X-as-a-service the default steady state, with teams consciously transitioning between them.

ideas.title: Reverse Conway maneuver
ideas.text: The book advises deliberately restructuring teams first, before a desired architecture change, since architecture tends to converge to match team boundaries.

try_it: Categorize your current teams against the four topologies and flag any team that doesn't cleanly fit one.
Write down your team's team API -- the concrete ways other teams should engage with you -- and share it with one adjacent team this week.
Audit your current cross-team dependencies and label each relationship as collaboration, X-as-a-service, or facilitation.
If you're planning an architecture change, sketch the team structure that would naturally produce that architecture and consider making that org change first.
best_for: Engineering directors and VPs restructuring a growing organization who need a shared vocabulary for team boundaries and hand-off points.
Platform and DevOps leaders trying to justify or scope an internal platform team without over-building it.
less_useful: Individual contributors or first-time managers without organizational design authority.
Small startups or single-team organizations, where the four-topology distinction adds overhead rather than clarity.

related.why: The Manager's Path addresses the individual career ladder inside the same kind of tech organization this book restructures.
The Unicorn Project dramatizes the same team-boundary and architecture problems this book formalizes.
